skills-reading: Read every map, table and chart in the same order: title, legend and units, source line, then the pattern. The units tell you whether you are looking at a total, a percent or a rate, which changes what you can claim. A strong pattern statement names real places and gives values, and a trend gives its direction, dates and size.
skills-scale: Geographers use "scale" in two ways. Map scale is the ratio between the map and the ground: a large-scale map shows a small area in detail. The scale of analysis is the size of the unit the data describe: global, regional, national or local. Name the scale from the data, not from the size of the map, and remember that a pattern at one scale can look different at another.
skills-frq: Free-response answers are scored part by part, one point each, against one rubric line. The task verb tells you what to write: identify names, define gives a meaning, describe gives features, explain gives the how or why with a link word, compare speaks of both sides and explain the degree states the degree first. Name a place and its scale whenever you can, and never just restate the question.
views-of-the-world: Maps are tools with jobs. Reference maps show where things are; thematic maps show a measure, using shades, dots, sized symbols, lines of equal value or resized areas. Every projection distorts shape, area, distance or direction, so choosing one is a trade-off. Maps show absolute and relative distance and direction, clustering and dispersal, and elevation.
data-sources: Geographic data are tied to places. Quantitative data are counts and measurements, from sources such as satellite images and GPS; qualitative data are words and pictures, from interviews, field notes, travel accounts, news and documents. Field observation gives rich local detail, remote sensing covers large areas over time, and a GIS layers data so geographers can see how they relate.
data-in-decisions: Census data and satellite images are powerful because decisions follow them: where a family buys a home, where a company opens a store, where a city lays pipes, how a country shares seats and money, and where aid goes after a disaster. They inform choices at every scale, from a block to the world. Every source also has limits: censuses age and undercount, satellites miss what clouds or roofs hide, and data for large areas hide what happens inside them.
spatial-concepts: Geographers locate places in two ways: absolutely, with latitude and longitude, and relatively, by what a place is near. Site is the character of the spot itself; situation is its links to other places, and both explain why places grow. Place is a location with meaning; space is how things are arranged across an area. Flows connect places, distance decay weakens contact with distance, and time-space compression makes far places feel closer.
human-environment: People and the environment shape each other. Natural resources can be renewable or nonrenewable, and how people use land changes the environment. Sustainability means using resources so they last for future users. Geographers once held environmental determinism, the idea that the environment decides how people live; they rejected it as wrong and as a cover for unequal rule, and moved to possibilism: the environment sets limits, and people choose.
scales-of-analysis: Geographers study patterns at the global, regional, national and local scales, naming the scale from the unit of the data. Aggregated data combine small units into large ones and hide variation, so a pattern at one scale can look different at another. Processes connect scales: global demand, trade and climate change reshape local places, and local choices respond. Always state the scale of a claim and match it to the question.
regional-analysis: Regions group places that share something. Formal regions share a measurable trait, functional regions are tied to a center by flows, and perceptual regions rest on what people believe. Regions exist at local, national, regional and global scales, usually fade out across transition zones, and can overlap or be contested, because people draw them for different purposes.
population-distribution: Population distribution is the pattern of where people live. Most of the world’s people live in a few clusters, in East Asia, South Asia and Europe, on low, well-watered land near coasts and rivers. Physical factors and human factors shape the pattern together, and the pattern looks different at the global, national and local scales.
distribution-consequences: Geographers measure crowding in three ways. Arithmetic density divides all people by all land; physiological density divides all people by arable land; agricultural density divides farmers by arable land. Carrying capacity, the number of people an area can support, is a different idea. Distribution and density affect services, society and the environment.
population-composition: A population pyramid shows a population’s age structure and sex ratio, one cohort per bar. An expansive pyramid has a wide base and a young, growing population; a constrictive one has a narrow base and falling births. Reading the shape tells planners what a place will need next, from schools to health care, and local pyramids can look very different from national ones.
population-dynamics: A population changes through births, deaths and migration. The crude birth and death rates give the rate of natural increase in percent, and the rule of 70 gives doubling time. The total fertility rate compared with replacement level (about 2.1) shows long-run growth or decline. Infant mortality and life expectancy measure health, and social, cultural, political and economic forces shape every rate.
transition-model: The demographic transition model describes death rates falling first and birth rates later, in five stages, so population growth speeds up and then slows or turns negative. The epidemiological transition describes the main causes of death shifting from infections to chronic disease. Both are models built from history, with limits: place a country’s data in a stage, and say how well the model fits.
malthusian-theory: Thomas Malthus argued in 1798 that population grows faster than food, so checks such as famine, disease and war would follow. Neo-Malthusians extend the worry to other resources. Three critiques stand out: technology raised food output, fertility fell as countries changed, and hunger depends on access to food more than total supply.
population-policies: Governments use pronatalist policies to raise births, antinatalist policies to lower them and immigration policies to decide who may move in. Policies can be voluntary or coercive and have intended and unintended effects. Many countries, including China (1980, 2016, 2021), Singapore and Iran, switched from lowering births to raising them as fertility fell.
women-population-change: More schooling, paid work, health care and contraception for women lower fertility and child deaths in most places, as in Bangladesh and Kerala, India. Changing roles also change who migrates. Ravenstein’s laws, drawn from 1800s British data, say most moves are short and step by step, every flow has a counterflow, and women moved more than men within their own country.
aging-populations: An aging population comes from fewer births and longer lives. The dependency ratio compares people under 15 and 65 and over with people of working age. Aging has economic, political and social effects, from worker shortages and pension debates to more care work in families, and it can be stronger in rural places that young people leave.
migration-causes: People migrate because of push factors at the place they leave and pull factors at the place they go, while intervening obstacles and opportunities along the way can block or redirect them. Causes can be cultural, demographic, economic, environmental or political, and most moves have more than one.
forced-voluntary-migration: Forced migrants are made to move, as refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons or, in the past, enslaved people. Voluntary migrants choose to move, within a country (internal, rural-to-urban) or abroad, in steps or along chains of relatives, as guest workers, as transnational migrants who keep ties to two countries, or seasonally with herds (transhumance).
migration-effects: Migration has economic, political, cultural and demographic effects on both the places people leave and the places they go. Origins gain remittances and may lose skills (brain drain) and young adults; destinations gain workers, new foods, languages and religions, and debate immigration policy. Name the place and the scale of every effect.
culture-intro: Culture is what a group learns and shares: practices, beliefs, objects and behaviors passed from one generation to the next. Culture traits include food, architecture and land use. Folk culture is small-group and slow to change; popular culture is widespread and fast-changing. Ethnocentrism judges another culture by your own standards, while cultural relativism seeks to understand it on its own terms, the habit geographers use.
culture-on-the-land: The cultural landscape is the human imprint on the land: buildings, fields, signs and places of worship. Landscapes build up in layers as each group leaves marks the next one reuses, which is sequent occupance. Architecture can be traditional (local styles and materials) or postmodern (mixed styles from about the 1970s on). Ethnicity, gender and Indigenous ways of life all shape space, from ethnic neighborhoods such as Little Saigon to the hogans of the Navajo Nation.
cultural-patterns: Language, religion and ethnicity are not spread evenly: they form regional patterns that you describe by naming where, what and how much. People shape their places through placemaking, which builds a sense of place. Cultural traits act as centripetal forces when they pull people together and centrifugal forces when they push them apart, and the same trait can do both at different scales, as Dutch and French do in Belgium.
diffusion-types: Diffusion is the spread of a trait from its hearth. In relocation diffusion people move and take the trait along. In expansion diffusion the trait spreads while it stays strong at home: contagiously to nearby people and places, hierarchically from large or powerful places to smaller ones (or the reverse), or as stimulus diffusion when the idea spreads but changes. Real cases often mix types, and distance decay and time-space compression shape how far and how fast a trait spreads.
diffusion-history: Long before the internet, trade, colonialism and imperialism moved culture across the world. Trade routes spread goods, words and skills; colonial powers spread their languages, religions and sports to the places they ruled, which is why Portuguese is spoken in Brazil and cricket is played in India. Where cultures met, new forms appeared: a lingua franca let different groups communicate, pidgins grew for trade and work, and creolization blended cultures into new languages and foods, such as Haitian Creole and Louisiana gumbo.
diffusion-today: Globalization links places through trade, travel, media and the internet, so traits now spread farther and faster than ever. Media, technology, politics, economics and social ties all carry culture, and growing cities mix people of many groups. The result is cultural convergence, as places share brands, media and English, and cultural divergence, as groups protect or revive their own culture. Indigenous languages are threatened when young people switch to dominant languages, yet laws, schools and new media can help them recover, as te reo Māori has in New Zealand.
religion-language-diffusion: Languages and religions spread from hearths, and maps, charts and place names show their paths. Languages belong to families of related languages, such as Indo-European, split into branches, languages and dialects. AP® Human Geography classes Christianity, Islam, Buddhism and Sikhism as universalizing religions, which spread by expansion and relocation, and Hinduism and Judaism as ethnic religions, which mostly stay near the hearth or spread by relocation. Religion figures come with a source and a year: Pew Research Center, 2025 report on 2020 data.
diffusion-effects: When diffusion brings cultures together, four results are common. In acculturation a group adds new traits and keeps its own. In assimilation its own traits fade away, by choice or by force. In syncretism traits blend into a new form, as in the Day of the Dead. In multiculturalism groups live side by side, each keeping its culture. Telling them apart comes down to one question: what happened to the original culture?
political-intro: States are the basic political units of the world: each has people, territory, a government and recognition by other states. Nations are peoples who share a culture. When one nation fills one state, the result is a nation-state; most states are multinational, some nations live in several states, and some, such as the Kurds, have no state at all. Autonomous regions govern many of their own affairs inside a larger state.
political-processes: Today's political map is the product of political processes. Colonialism and imperialism put much of the world under European rule and drew many borders. Independence movements used the idea of self-determination to win sovereign states, most of them between 1945 and 1975. The new states mostly kept their colonial borders, and large states such as the Soviet Union later broke apart into new ones.
power-territoriality: Political power means control over people, land, resources and routes. Territoriality is how people, groups and states claim and mark areas, at every scale from a fenced yard to a guarded national border. Neocolonialism is influence over former colonies without direct rule. Choke points, such as the Suez Canal and the Strait of Hormuz, give power over trade, and shatterbelts are regions where outside powers compete.
defining-boundaries: Political boundaries mark where one state's territory ends. Geographers sort them by history: antecedent boundaries come before settlement and subsequent ones after; consequent boundaries follow cultural lines and geometric ones follow straight lines; superimposed boundaries are forced by outside powers, and relict boundaries no longer work but still show on the land. Many boundaries fit more than one type.
boundary-functions: Boundaries are defined, delimited, demarcated and administered, and they are often disputed. They control the flow of people and goods, from open borders in the Schengen Area to the closed Korean DMZ. Many African borders go back to the Berlin Conference era. At sea, the law of the sea sets a territorial sea to 12 nautical miles, a contiguous zone to 24 and an exclusive economic zone to 200, beyond which lie the high seas.
internal-boundaries: Internal boundaries divide a state into smaller units, including voting districts. Redistricting redraws those districts, in the United States after each census, at the national, state and local scales. Gerrymandering draws them to favor one side: packing wastes a party's votes in a few lopsided districts, and cracking spreads them too thin to win. Independent commissions and rules for compact districts make it harder.
forms-of-governance: States share power across space in two main ways. A unitary state concentrates power in the national government, which gives regions only the powers it chooses. A federal state divides power by constitution between a national government and regional governments, so laws differ from region to region. Large or culturally diverse states are often federal, and both forms always keep a national government.
devolution-factors: Devolution moves power from a national government to its regions. It is pushed by physical division, ethnic separatism, ethnic cleansing, terrorism, economic and social problems, and irredentism. A minority concentrated in its own region, as in Quebec, Scotland or Catalonia, is the most common source of pressure. Most devolution ends with more regional self-rule, but some states break apart, as Pakistan did in 1971.
sovereignty-challenges: Sovereignty is challenged from below and above. Devolution can create autonomous regions and subnational units, as in Spain, Belgium, Canada and Nigeria, or break a state apart, as with Sudan and the Soviet Union. Supranational organizations such as the UN, NATO, the EU, ASEAN, the African Union and the Arctic Council help states face shared problems, gain larger markets and defend each other, but limit what each member decides alone. Communication technology speeds all of these changes, including democratization.
centrifugal-centripetal: Centrifugal forces pull a state apart; centripetal forces hold it together. When centrifugal forces win, the results can include uneven development, ethnic nationalist movements, stateless nations and even failed states such as Somalia after 1991. When centripetal forces win, the results include a shared identity, fairer sharing of roads, services and money, and cultural cohesion. The same trait can pull in both directions at different scales.
agriculture-intro: Agriculture is the purposeful raising of crops and animals. Intensive farming puts many inputs into each hectare; extensive farming spreads few inputs over large areas. Climate shapes which kind fits a place, and irrigation lets people farm beyond what rain allows.
settlement-survey: Rural settlements are clustered, dispersed or linear. Survey methods divide land: metes and bounds follows natural features, township and range makes a square grid, and long lots run in strips from a river. The method used often shaped the settlement pattern, as the grid did in the US Midwest.
agricultural-origins: Domestication turned wild species into crops and livestock in several hearths, including the Fertile Crescent, the Indus valley, Southeast Asia and Central America. Farming led to settled villages and surpluses. After 1492 the Columbian Exchange carried crops, animals and diseases between the hemispheres.
second-agricultural-revolution: The Second Agricultural Revolution, from the 1700s in Britain and the 1800s in North America, brought crop rotation, selective breeding, enclosure and mechanization. Each farm worker grew more food, diets and life spans improved, and people no longer needed on farms moved to towns.
green-revolution: The Green Revolution, from the 1960s to the 1980s, spread high-yield wheat and rice with fertilizer, irrigation and pesticides. It raised food output and weakened Malthus's prediction, but it used much water and chemicals, favored larger farmers and spread unevenly. GMOs came later, in the late 1990s.
production-regions: Subsistence agriculture feeds the farm family; commercial agriculture sells for profit and often uses monocropping. Bid-rent theory explains why intensive uses take costly land near a market and extensive uses take cheap, distant land, though real regions with many markets and routes depart from it.
farm-organization: Large commercial operations have been replacing family farms because economies of scale lower their costs. Agribusiness links farms to the firms that supply and buy from them along commodity chains, and technology has raised yields and carrying capacity while shrinking rural communities.
von-thunen: The von Thünen model explains farm land use by the cost of transport to one market, producing rings of market gardening and dairy, forest, grain and ranching. It assumes an isolated, uniform plain and transport by cart; refrigeration, air freight, specialty farming and many markets break the rings in real regions.
global-agriculture: Global supply chains link farms, processors, shippers and stores across countries, and they are more than transport. Countries that depend on one or a few raw farm exports face price swings, and food distribution depends on politics, trade, transport and income as well as on how much is grown.
agriculture-consequences: Farming changes landscapes through slash and burn, deforestation, terracing, irrigation and wetland draining. Its environmental effects include pollution, salinization, desertification and habitat loss, offset in part by conservation practices. Its societal effects include changing diets, the purpose of farming and who does the work.
agriculture-challenges: Farming faces debates over GMOs and aquaculture, and shoppers drive movements such as organic, local food, CSA, urban farming, value-added crops and fair trade. Food insecurity and food deserts come mostly from poverty, conflict, distribution, weather and lost farmland, not from too little food.
women-in-agriculture: Women's farm labor covers every stage of the food system and differs by place and type of production. FAO data show women make up a large share of agrifood workers in Southern Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, and gaps in pay, land rights and access to inputs, not ability, hold back their output.
urbanization-origins: Cities first grew where farming produced a food surplus, mostly in river valleys. Site (the physical place) explains where a city starts; situation (its links to other places) explains much of how it grows, and situation can change. Urbanization, a rising share of people in cities, is driven by transport, communication, population growth, migration, development and policy.
cities-worldwide: Megacities (10 million or more) and metacities (20 million or more) are multiplying, mostly in Asia and Africa. In the United States and other high-income countries, cities spread outward instead: suburbanization and sprawl produced edge cities (suburban job centers), boomburbs (fast-growing suburban cities) and exurbs (commuter homes among farms).
cities-globalization: World cities sit at the top of the urban hierarchy because they host the headquarters, banks, law firms, media and international bodies that steer the world economy. They form a network linked by flows of money, information and people, and decisions made in them spread down the hierarchy and out to places at every scale.
city-size-distribution: The rank-size rule predicts a smooth ladder of city sizes; a primate city breaks it, usually because a capital or colonial port gathered power and money. The gravity model predicts more interaction between big, close places. Central place theory explains the spacing of settlements from threshold and range. All four are models that fit some countries better than others.
city-structure: Urban models describe how land use is arranged inside cities. North American models move from one center (concentric zone, sector) to many (multiple nuclei, galactic city) as cars spread. Latin American, Southeast Asian and African city models show how colonial history and fast growth create other patterns, such as squatter settlements at the edge. Each fits some cities and fails in others.
density-land-use: Housing and land use reflect culture, technology and the cycles of building and decline that every city goes through. Residential density is usually highest near the center and falls toward the edge. Zoning rules lock in density patterns, and infilling adds new buildings on empty lots inside the built-up area.
infrastructure: Infrastructure is the network of transport, utilities, communications and public buildings that lets a place function. Where it is located and how good it is shape where firms invest, where people can live and how healthy and connected they are, so it shapes patterns of economic and social development at every scale.
urban-sustainability: Urban sustainability policies try to meet a city's needs without wasting land, energy or money. Smart growth tools (mixed use, walkability, transit-oriented development, New Urbanism, greenbelts and growth boundaries, slow-growth caps) can cut sprawl and driving, but critics point to higher housing costs, possible segregation and loss of historic character.
urban-data: Urban geographers study change with quantitative data (census and survey counts of people, housing, income and travel) and qualitative data (interviews, field observation and residents' narratives). Numbers show what changed and how much; qualitative data show why and what it means. Each has limits, so strong answers use both and name the scale of the data.
urban-change-challenges: US cities were shaped by redlining and blockbusting, which drained investment from some neighborhoods; by urban renewal, which cleared many of them; and by gentrification, which brings investment and displacement. Around the world, squatter settlements face insecure land rights and poor services, and pollution often falls hardest on poorer communities. Cities respond with inclusionary zoning, fair-lending laws, land titles, local food projects and regional planning.
sustainability-challenges: Growing cities face sprawl, poor sanitation, air and water pollution, high energy use and climate risks such as heat and flooding. Their ecological footprints reach far beyond their limits. Cities respond by cleaning up and reusing brownfields, drawing growth boundaries, protecting farmland and planning across a whole metro area, and each response has trade-offs.
industrial-revolution: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 1700s, when new machines and steam power met coal and iron. Factories clustered in towns, farmworkers moved to cities, a working class formed, and the hunt for raw materials and markets fed colonialism.
economic-sectors: Jobs fall into five sectors, from taking resources from nature to making the top decisions. Factories locate to keep total costs low: weight-losing industries near raw materials, weight-gaining ones near markets, and processing at break-of-bulk points. Core countries have mostly service and research jobs; the periphery more primary work.
development-measures: Development is measured with income measures (GDP, GNP, GNI per capita), social measures (fertility, infant mortality, literacy, health care, energy use) and composites: the HDI (health, education, income) and the GII (gaps between women and men, lower is better). Each shows something and hides something, such as inequality and the informal sector.
women-development: As places develop, more women go to school and take paid work, as in Bangladesh's garment industry, but a gender wage gap and unequal opportunity remain. Microlending, pioneered by the Grameen Bank, gives small loans for small businesses, mostly to women: it can raise income and schooling, but it is no cure for poverty on its own.
development-theories: Rostow's stages say every country can climb one path from traditional society to high mass consumption. World system theory sees one world economy of core, semiperiphery and periphery. Dependency theory blames the periphery's poverty on its ties to the core. Commodity dependence ties a country to one export's price. Each model has assumptions and limits.
trade-world-economy: Trade happens where places complement each other. Comparative advantage, the lower opportunity cost, decides who should make what, even when one country has the absolute advantage in everything. Neoliberal policies, tariffs, the WTO, trade blocs such as the EU and Mercosur, OPEC and IMF loans shape trade and make the world economy interdependent.
world-economy-changes: Cheaper transport and communication let firms outsource work, so older industrial regions deindustrialized while newly industrialized countries grew, often in special economic zones. Production split into an international division of labor run on post-Fordist, just-in-time methods. Agglomeration clusters firms; a growth pole spreads growth outward through the multiplier effect.
sustainable-development: Sustainable development improves lives now without harming future generations. Resource depletion, mass consumption, pollution and climate change make it hard. The UN Sustainable Development Goals (2015, for 2030) set shared targets, and ecotourism can make protecting nature pay, though it has limits. Responses work at global, national and local scales.
